f: Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate
m: The minimum interest rate a bank used to set for floating-rate loans, worked out from its own latest cost of funds. RBI introduced it in April 2016.
e: Many home loans taken between 2016 and 2019 are still linked to the bank's MCLR, so their EMI changes when the bank revises its MCLR.

m: A floating loan rate linked to an outside benchmark, usually the RBI repo rate. Since October 2019, new retail and MSME floating loans in India must use one.
e: If the RBI cuts the repo rate, a repo-linked home loan becomes cheaper much faster than an old MCLR-linked loan.

m: The older minimum lending rate banks used before MCLR. It applied from 2010 until MCLR replaced it in 2016.
e: Some very old loans still run on the base rate, and borrowers are often advised to switch to a newer benchmark.

f: Current Account and Savings Account Ratio
m: The share of a bank's deposits that sit in current and savings accounts. These deposits pay little interest, so a higher CASA ratio means cheaper money for the bank.
e: Analysts like banks with a high CASA ratio because they can lend profitably even when interest rates fall.

m: A company that gives loans or other financial services but is not a bank. It is regulated by the RBI but cannot issue cheques drawn on itself or take demand deposits like a bank.
e: Bajaj Finance gives consumer loans to buy phones and TVs, but it is an NBFC, not a bank.

f: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
m: An Indian law that lets banks take possession of and sell the security given against a loan after a default, without going to court first.
e: After a borrower stopped paying a secured business loan, the bank used the SARFAESI Act to take over and auction the pledged factory.

m: India's law for resolving companies that cannot pay their debts, through a time-bound process that tries to revive the company or else sell its assets.
e: Under the IBC, lenders of a failing steel company accepted a new owner's resolution plan instead of letting the plant shut down.

m: A special tribunal that hears company law matters in India, including insolvency cases under the IBC, mergers and disputes between shareholders.
e: A bank filed an insolvency case against the defaulting company at the NCLT in Mumbai.

m: A business form that mixes a partnership with limited liability: partners run the business together, but each partner's personal assets are protected from the firm's debts.
e: Three CA friends registered their practice as an LLP so that one partner's mistake would not put the others' homes at risk.

m: Smaller businesses, classified in India by their investment in plant and machinery and their annual turnover. They get special support such as easier credit and government schemes.
e: A family-run spare-parts unit in Ludhiana registers as an MSME to get cheaper loans and faster payments from big buyers.

m: The free online registration that gives an Indian business official MSME status, in place since July 2020.
e: Before applying for a government tender, Ravi completed his Udyam Registration in a few minutes using his Aadhaar and PAN.

m: The government's online marketplace where ministries, departments and PSUs buy goods and services directly from registered sellers.
e: A small furniture maker in Jaipur now sells office chairs to government offices across India through GeM.

m: An electronic document generated on the GST portal that is needed to move goods worth more than the set limit (generally ₹50,000) from one place to another.
e: The truck carrying ₹3 lakh of fabric from Surat to Delhi must carry a valid e-way bill, or it can be stopped and fined.

m: Under GST, a business can reduce the tax it pays on sales by the GST it has already paid on its purchases.
e: A bakery pays ₹1,000 GST on flour and charges ₹1,800 GST on cakes, so it pays only ₹800 to the government after claiming input tax credit.

m: An international numbering system used to classify goods. Under GST, the HSN code on an invoice decides the tax rate.
e: Writing the wrong HSN code on an invoice can mean charging the wrong GST rate and getting a tax notice.

m: A certificate your employer gives you every year showing your salary and the income tax (TDS) deducted from it. You use it to file your income tax return.
e: In June, Neha downloads her Form 16 from the HR portal and uses it to file her ITR.

m: The form you file with the Income Tax Department to report your income for the year and the tax you have paid or still owe.
e: Even fresh graduates who earn above the exemption limit must file an ITR, and filing helps later when applying for loans or visas.

m: A three-digit credit score from 300 to 900, given by TransUnion CIBIL, that shows how reliably you repay loans and credit card bills.
e: With a CIBIL score above 750, Aman got his education loan approved quickly and at a lower interest rate.

m: An account that holds your shares, bonds and mutual fund units in electronic form, instead of paper certificates.
e: To buy her first shares, Simran opened a demat account and a trading account with a broker.

m: Shares and money are exchanged one working day after the trade. Indian stock markets moved fully to T+1 settlement in January 2023.
e: If you sell shares on Monday, the money reaches your trading account on Tuesday under T+1 settlement.

m: Derivative contracts whose value depends on an underlying share or index. Traders use them to hedge risk or to bet on price moves with borrowed leverage.
e: SEBI studies have found that most individual traders in F&O lose money, which is why it warns beginners to be careful.

m: The maximum price a share is allowed to rise to in one trading day. Trading at the top of the band pauses or slows once it is hit.
e: After strong results, the small-cap stock hit its 20% upper circuit within minutes of the market opening.

m: The lowest price a share is allowed to fall to in one trading day, set by the exchange to stop panic selling.
e: After news of a fraud at the company, its shares were stuck at the lower circuit with almost no buyers.

m: A single very large trade between two parties, done in a separate trading window on the stock exchange so that it does not disturb the normal market.
e: A foreign fund sold a big stake in an Indian bank through a block deal early in the morning.

m: A way for promoters or the government to sell their existing shares in a listed company to the public through the stock exchange.
e: The government sold part of its stake in a PSU through an OFS, with a portion kept aside for retail investors.

m: When a company that is already listed issues new shares to the public to raise more money.
e: After its IPO a few years earlier, the company launched an FPO to fund a new plant.

m: A quick way for a listed Indian company to raise money by selling shares only to large institutional investors such as mutual funds and insurance companies.
e: The bank raised ₹5,000 crore through a QIP in two days to strengthen its capital.

m: The first time a new mutual fund scheme is open for investment, usually at ₹10 per unit.
e: An NFO priced at ₹10 is not automatically cheaper than an existing fund. What matters is what the fund invests in.

m: The price of one unit of a mutual fund, worked out daily as the fund's assets minus its liabilities, divided by the number of units.
e: If you invest ₹10,000 when the NAV is ₹50, you get 200 units of the fund.

m: The yearly fee a mutual fund charges, shown as a percentage of your investment. It is deducted from the fund's value.
e: Over 20 years, a fund with a 0.5% expense ratio can leave you with noticeably more money than a similar fund charging 2%.

m: A tax-saving equity mutual fund with a three-year lock-in. Investments qualify for deduction under Section 80C in the old tax regime.
e: Karan invests in an ELSS fund every month to save tax and build long-term wealth at the same time.

m: A long-term, government-backed savings scheme with a 15-year lock-in, a fixed interest rate set by the government, and tax benefits.
e: Parents often open a PPF account early to build a safe fund for their child's higher education.

m: The final payment a company makes to an employee who leaves: pending salary, leave encashment and bonus, minus any amounts owed to the company.
e: Two months after resigning, Priya received her full and final settlement along with her relieving letter.

m: A letter from your employer confirming that you have left the job properly and have been released from your duties. New employers often ask for it.
e: The new company would not confirm Arjun's joining until he submitted the relieving letter from his last job.

m: A formal plan given to an employee whose performance is below expectations, with clear goals and a deadline to improve.
e: After missing targets for two quarters, Rohit was put on a 60-day PIP with weekly check-ins with his manager.

m: A contract some employers ask freshers to sign, promising to stay for a fixed period or pay a penalty for leaving early, usually because the company paid for their training.
e: Before signing an offer with a two-year bond, read exactly how much you would have to pay if you leave early.

m: In IT and consulting firms, employees 'on the bench' are on the payroll but not assigned to any client project at the moment.
e: While on the bench for a month, Sneha used the time to complete a cloud certification.

m: A full-time job offer given to a student by the company where they did their internship, before the regular placement season starts.
e: After a strong summer internship at an FMCG company, Vikram received a PPO and skipped the placement season.

m: The first and most competitive day of campus placements, when top recruiters usually visit and make offers.
e: Students prepare for months for Day Zero because the best-paying companies come on that day.

m: How much profit a company earns for every rupee of shareholders' money: net profit divided by shareholders' equity.
e: A company that earns ₹20 crore profit on ₹100 crore of equity has an ROE of 20%.

m: How efficiently a company uses all its long-term capital, from both equity and debt: operating profit (EBIT) divided by capital employed.
e: Investors compare ROCE across cement companies to see which one earns more from every rupee of capital it uses.

m: The average return a company must pay to all its investors, lenders and shareholders, weighted by how much each one provides.
e: If a new project is expected to return 10% but the company's WACC is 12%, the project destroys value.
